text.p: Reserve Bank Governor Bernie Fraser made several unambiguously bullish comments on Thursday in his final annual appearance before the House of Representative's Committee on Financial Institutions and Public Administration.
Fraser clearly thinks the economy can safely grow faster than it is at present.
Further, the bank has obviously developed rock-solid confidence on inflation, contrasting with doubts it holds about unemployment, which is now clearly rising.
And most spectacularly, he said inflation is no constraint on growth -- which is an extraordinarily positive thing for a central bank governor to say, even a retiring one.
Canberra Watch found these three quotes the most revealing:
"Can we grow faster? We probably can, given the spare capacity in plants and in the labout market."
"(Inflation and the current account deficit) are the two traditional constraints that have caused growth to slow down in the past. They're not constraints at the moment."
"We are a bit more confident about what might happen on inflation over the next six or 12 months than we are about what might happen to growth and employment."
Fraser also agreed with former treasurer Ralph Willis who suggested that further rate cuts would be a consequence of the economy needing support.
Fraser's only qualification was that the inflation outlook would have to be comfortable, and he clearly thinks it is.
Notably, Fraser's bearish comments were mostly routine ones -- the things that he always says, because he's a central bank governor and he has to recite the textbook every time he speaks.
One does not take too much notice of those warnings unless he seems to be repeating them more often than usual, and on Thursday he did not.
The remarks that were out of the ordinary tended to be bullish.
Take, for example, the comments on wages, the subject that was the monetary bogeyman a few months ago:
Fraser -- "... at least for the time being we think that wage increases are under control."

Macfarlane -- "... it would be extremely unfortunate if wage settlements, if the trade union movement were to aim for an average increase in wage settlements which was not consistent with that (the inflation target). I don't think they will."
And Fraser said in his prepared opening remarks that the bank was more bullish on through-year inflation than is the government, which is forecasting 2.75 percent for the June quarter.
One remark that has attracted a lot of attention but which is really unimportant is his long-term crystal-balling on an unemployment target.

This was a response to a committee member asking a purely theoretical question about what would be an achievable target for unemployment. Implicitly, the concern here is the NAIRU -- the non-accelerating-inflation rate of unemployment.
Fraser said that Australia could aim for five or six percent and see what happened, if it got there.
This is hardly surprising. Bernie Fraser is not the type to seek slow growth simply because, somewhere out there (though we don't know where), lurks the nasty NAIRU monster.
The quotes are getting media attention only because the political debate in Canberra is currently pursuing the puerile issue of the government refusing to set an unemployment target.
The former government had a target that no-one thought it would ever achieve.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
